name: Headwaters Forest Defense v. County of Humboldt
court: Ninth Circuit (from the Northern District of California, District Judge Vaughn R. Walker)
citation: 240 F.3d 1185 (9th Cir. 2000) (amended opinion), vacated and remanded, 534 U.S. 801 (2001); on remand, 276 F.3d 1125 (9th Cir. 2002)
decided: May 4, 2000; amended January 31, 2001; vacated and remanded by the Supreme Court in 2001; opinion on remand filed January 11, 2002, corrected January 30, 2002
topic: Fourth Amendment excessive force, pepper spray applied with cotton swabs to the closed eyes and sprayed into the faces of nonviolent protesters locked together with steel devices, pain compliance against passive resisters, supervisors who authorized the tactic, judgment as a matter of law after a hung jury reversed, qualified immunity denied on remand after Saucier
summary: Humboldt County deputies, acting under a tactic authorized by the sheriff and chief deputy, swabbed pepper spray into the eyes of nonviolent logging protesters who had locked themselves together with steel sleeves, then sprayed some of them in the face from inches away and withheld water until they released. The Ninth Circuit reversed a judgment entered for the defendants after a hung jury, holding that pepper spray is more than a minimal intrusion, that a pain compliance technique on nonviolent protesters is reasonable only if the governmental interest is particularly strong, and that reasonableness was for the jury. After the Supreme Court vacated and remanded in light of Saucier, the panel held that no reasonable officer could have thought the force reasonable and denied the sheriff and chief deputy qualified immunity. It is the Ninth Circuit's leading case on pepper spray and passive resistance.

The course describes protesters locked to logs. The opinions describe protesters locked to each other with steel devices in a lumber company lobby, locked to bulldozers at a logging site, and locked around a tree stump brought into a congressman's office. No subsequent history after the 2002 remand was checked.
facts:
The case arose from a nine day jury trial, so the facts are the trial evidence viewed in the light most favorable to the protesters, as the court was required to view it in reviewing judgment as a matter of law.

In the fall of 1997, environmental activists staged three nonviolent protests against logging of old growth redwoods in Humboldt County. At each, two to seven protesters linked themselves together with devices called black bears: steel cylinders weighing ten to twenty-five pounds with a center post, into which the protesters put their arms and clipped their wrist bracelets with climbing carabiners. The protesters could release themselves from inside. Officers could remove the devices with a hand held electric grinder, and one deputy had done so hundreds of times without injury. Citing concern about sparks, Sheriff Dennis Lewis and Chief Deputy Gary Philp decided over the summer of 1997 that use of a lock down device by any protester, however peaceful, was active resistance warranting pepper spray as a pain compliance technique. The sheriff conceded at trial that no agency in the county, the state or the nation had ever used pepper spray on nonviolent protesters this way; the state attorney general described its use as previously limited to hostile or violent subjects.

Scotia, September 27: seven protesters sat in a circle in the Pacific Lumber lobby. Officers made no attempt to negotiate. After repeated warnings, they forced four protesters' heads back and applied pepper spray with cotton swabs to the corners of their closed eyes. The protesters screamed. Three others released and were handcuffed and left on a couch nearby. The four were swabbed again; water was offered twenty minutes after the first application. Officers then carried the remaining pairs out on stretchers in about three minutes each and ground off the last device in ten minutes with a fire blanket over the protesters.

Bear Creek, October 3: two pairs locked to bulldozers. The officer in charge told them spray would be used because it was quicker, waited more than half an hour for a videographer, gave a five minute warning but applied spray in under two, swabbed two protesters' eyes, told them they would get water only if they released, and a minute later sprayed both in the face in short full bursts from inches away. He said they had all day and all kinds of cans. A grinder was then used safely despite the fuel cans the officers had cited as the reason not to use it.

Riggs, October 16: four young women, one a minor, locked around a tree stump in a congressman's office with wood chips on the floor. A vacuum was offered and declined. Protesters pleaded that they posed no danger. Officers swabbed their eyes; one protester testified her eyes were pried open, which the defendants denied. Water was conditioned on release. An officer sprayed one woman in the face from a foot away. All released within minutes.

No protester sought medical treatment. The district court granted qualified immunity to all individual officers except Lewis and Philp before trial, granted it to those two at the close of the plaintiffs' case, declared a mistrial when the jury deadlocked after six hours, set a new trial, and eight weeks later entered judgment as a matter of law for the county, the city and their departments.
holding:
The 2000 opinion, as amended in 2001, reversed the judgment as a matter of law and the grant of qualified immunity to Lewis and Philp and remanded for a new trial.

Standard. Reasonableness under Graham is ordinarily a question of fact for the jury, and judgment as a matter of law is proper only if the evidence allows one reasonable conclusion. The district court had resolved conflicts against the nonmoving parties, which was error. The court distinguished Forrester v. City of San Diego, where the question was whether substantial evidence supported a jury verdict that nunchaku pain compliance was reasonable; here the question was whether a reasonable jury could find pepper spray excessive.

Nature of the intrusion. The district court had called the force the infliction of transient pain without significant risk of injury and therefore minimal. The court disagreed. The absence of injury is not dispositive; nominal damages are available for an unreasonable intrusion on bodily integrity, and the risk of injury is only one factor. The county's own chemical agent trainer testified that pepper spray is designed to cause intense pain, a burning sensation, mucus discharge, involuntary eye closure, gagging and temporary paralysis of the larynx, with disorientation, anxiety and panic. Unlike the nunchaku in Forrester, whose gradual pressure officers could moderate and release the moment the subject complied, pepper spray produced immediate and searing pain that officers could not stop once the protesters agreed to release; the only relief is thorough flushing with water, which officers delayed or conditioned on release and delivered in spray bottle bursts that may have made it worse. Forrester did not hold that pain compliance techniques are constitutionally permissible as a matter of law, and the court held that whether this pepper spray use was excessive was for the jury.

Governmental interests. Speedy removal was not supported: the spray prolonged each incident and physical removal took minutes. The organized lawlessness rationale failed because every officer testified the decision rested solely on the difficulty of using the grinder, and because a handful of protesters inside a building, separated from peaceful crowds outside, was not a menacing group; abstract notions of law and order cannot justify force the facts do not. The protesters' use of lock down devices did not meet the Eureka Police Department's own definition of active resistance, which required attempting to inflict pain or injury on the officer. The protesters, mostly young women, two of them minors, were nonviolent, unarmed and not menacing; they posed no threat to themselves or anyone else, which is the most important factor. There was no split second judgment: the decision to spray anyone in a lock down device was made before officers were called to any scene. The crime was trespass, a misdemeanor that militates against significant force on a nonviolent subject. Alternatives (negotiation, the grinder, carrying the protesters out, waiting) were supported by considerable evidence that the district court dismissed out of hand. The court summarized: using such a pain compliance technique to arrest nonviolent protesters can be reasonable only if the countervailing governmental interests are particularly strong, and the evidence showed the opposite. It expressly did not decide whether the force was in fact excessive, only that the question belonged to the jury.

Qualified immunity in the first opinion. The law was clearly established under Graham and Mendoza v. Block (an officer does not get immunity every time a novel method is used to inflict injury). Because historical facts were disputed about the amount of force (closed or open eyes, the need for swabs and full blasts, distance, water, pain) and about the justification (threat, active resistance, alternatives), and about what Lewis and Philp knew and authorized (full blasts versus swabs only, the limited scope of the district attorney's opinion, their knowledge that state policy limited pepper spray to hostile or violent subjects), immunity could not be decided as a matter of law.

On remand after Saucier (2002). The Supreme Court vacated and remanded for reconsideration under Saucier's two step sequence. The panel reaffirmed. Step one: viewing the facts for the protesters, Lewis and Philp violated the Fourth Amendment. Step two: it would be clear to a reasonable officer that the force was excessive, because the spray was unnecessary to subdue, remove or arrest the protesters, they could be safely carried out and ground free in minutes without pain, and calling their conduct active resistance was contrary to the facts. The repeated applications were also clearly unreasonable under LaLonde v. County of Riverside, decided before the incidents: once an arrestee is helpless, continued use of pepper spray or a refusal without cause to alleviate its effects is excessive. Authorizing full blasts despite the manufacturer's warning against spraying within three feet, and withholding water for over twenty minutes or until release, were clearly excessive. The panel held that the use of pepper spray on the protesters' eyes and faces was plainly in excess of the force necessary under the circumstances and no reasonable officer could have concluded otherwise, and remanded consistent with its earlier reversal of judgment for the municipalities.
notDecided:
Whether the force was in fact excessive. The 2000 opinion stated expressly that it was not deciding that question, only that the district court erred in taking it from the jury. The 2002 opinion decided the qualified immunity question for Lewis and Philp on the protesters' version of the facts; it did not decide the merits against them.

The liability of the line officers who applied the spray. The district court's pretrial grant of qualified immunity to them was not before the court; the appeal concerned Lewis and Philp and the municipal defendants.

Whether pepper spray is permissible on passive resisters in other settings. The court distinguished Forrester (protesters physically blocking a clinic, pain compliance that could be moderated) and did not hold pain compliance unlawful as such.

Municipal liability. The court reversed the judgment for the county and city and remanded for a new trial; it did not find a policy or custom.

The final result on remand is not recorded in the opinions read.
inPractice:
Headwaters is the case that fixes pepper spray on the force scale in the Ninth Circuit. The court rejected the idea that pain without lasting injury is a minimal intrusion. Officers should expect pepper spray to be treated as a significant use of force, as the Ninth Circuit later confirmed in Young, and should justify it with the same Graham factors as any other tool.

The second lesson is about pain compliance on passive subjects. The court's distinction from Forrester turned on control: the nunchaku could be tightened gradually and released the instant the subject complied, while pepper spray, once applied, kept hurting whether the subject complied or not, and officers could only relieve it with water. A pain compliance technique that the officer cannot stop on compliance is a poor fit for a passive resister, and using it on protesters who posed no threat and could be carried out and cut free was, on remand, held plainly excessive.

Third, the definition of resistance matters. The agencies' own policies defined active resistance as trying to hurt the officer, and the court held the sheriff to that definition. Locking arms into a device is an obstacle to arrest, not an attack.

Fourth, the opinion is a warning to supervisors. Lewis and Philp authorized the tactic in advance. The court looked at what they knew (state policy limited the spray to hostile or violent subjects, the district attorney had declined to opine on civil liability, no one had used the spray this way) and at what they failed to control (full blasts from inches away, no instruction on reapplication intervals, water withheld). Pre-authorizing a tool for a category of subjects, without regard to the facts on scene, removed the split second defense entirely.

Dr. Sowards teaches Headwaters in the less lethal line with Deorle, Bryan and Young, and as the case that separates passive resistance from active resistance for chemical agents.
trainIt:
Teach pepper spray as intermediate force. Students should be able to recite what the county's own trainer said it does, and should understand that the absence of medical treatment did not make the intrusion minimal in the court's eyes.

Teach the control test for pain compliance. Have students compare a wrist lock or nunchaku, which the officer can tighten and release, with a chemical agent, which continues to act after compliance. Ask which is appropriate for a seated, passive subject who is not a threat, and why. The court's answer was that the uncontrollable nature of the pain, plus the inability to stop it on compliance, made pepper spray a different kind of tool.

Teach decontamination as part of the force. Water withheld for twenty minutes, or offered only on release, was treated by the court as part of the excessive force, under LaLonde. Students must know that relief after exposure is a duty, not a bargaining chip, and that spray bottle mists may not be adequate.

Teach the alternatives analysis. Negotiate, cut the device, carry the subject out, or wait. Students should be able to list the alternatives available at each of the three protests and explain why the court found the evidence of them sufficient to go to a jury. Removal took six minutes once the officers decided to do it.

Teach the supervisor's exposure. Walk through what Lewis and Philp knew and what they did not direct: distances, reapplication, water. Have supervisors in the class write the authorization they would have issued instead, with limits on application method, distance, interval and decontamination, and with a requirement that the on scene facts, not the category of protest, justify the force.

Teach the posture honestly: a hung jury, a judgment for the defendants reversed, a Supreme Court vacatur, and a reaffirmed denial of qualified immunity for the two supervisors on the protesters' version of the facts. No court in these opinions found anyone liable.
caution: Two opinions were read: the amended 2000 opinion (240 F.3d 1185) and the 2002 opinion after remand (276 F.3d 1125). The 2000 opinion's judgment was vacated by the Supreme Court in light of Saucier, so its qualified immunity analysis (which merged the immunity question with the merits under then current circuit law) is superseded by the 2002 opinion, although later Ninth Circuit cases continue to cite its excessive force discussion. The original May 4, 2000 slip opinion was not available in the archive and was not read; the archive stub points to the amended version. The archive texts have no reporter pagination. The facts are the plaintiffs' version viewed as required on review of judgment as a matter of law; the defendants disputed whether eyes were opened, whether water was offered, and the alternatives available. The course description of protesters locked to logs does not match the opinions, which describe steel devices linking protesters to each other, to bulldozers and around a tree stump.

applications.title: Pain without injury is still force
applications.body: The court rejected the district court's view that transient pain without risk of injury is a minimal intrusion. Pepper spray is designed to cause intense pain, involuntary eye closure, gagging and larynx paralysis. Justify it like any other significant force.

applications.title: Passive resistance is not active resistance
applications.body: The agencies' own policy defined active resistance as attempting to inflict pain or injury on the officer. Protesters locked into devices, sitting peacefully, met neither that definition nor the court's. An obstacle to arrest is not an attack.

applications.title: Pain compliance you cannot stop
applications.body: Nunchaku in Forrester could be tightened gradually and released on compliance. Pepper spray kept burning after the protesters agreed to release, and only water relieved it. The court treated that difference as central to whether a pain compliance technique fit a nonviolent subject.

applications.title: Decontamination is part of the force
applications.body: Withholding water for twenty minutes, or conditioning it on release, was held clearly excessive under LaLonde. Once a subject is helpless, refusing without cause to alleviate the effects of a chemical agent is itself excessive force.

applications.title: A pre-authorized tactic has no split second defense
applications.body: The decision to spray any protester in a lock down device was made before officers were called to any scene. The court held Graham's allowance for rapidly evolving situations did not apply, and looked hard at what the authorizing supervisors knew.

applications.title: Posture
applications.body: The jury hung, the trial court entered judgment for the defendants, the Ninth Circuit reversed and ordered a new trial, the Supreme Court vacated for reconsideration under Saucier, and the panel reaffirmed that the sheriff and chief deputy were not entitled to qualified immunity on the protesters' facts. No opinion read found anyone liable.

quiz.q: How did the Ninth Circuit respond to the district court's characterization of pepper spray as the infliction of transient pain without significant risk of physical injury, and therefore a minimal intrusion?
options: It disagreed, holding that the absence of injury is not dispositive and that the evidence of intense pain, involuntary eye closure, gagging and panic allowed a jury to find the intrusion more than minimal
It held pepper spray is deadly force
It held the question irrelevant because the protesters were trespassing
quiz.teach: The court relied on the county's own chemical agent trainer's description of the spray's effects and on the rule that a plaintiff may recover nominal damages for an unreasonable intrusion on bodily integrity even without injury.

quiz.q: What distinction did the court draw between the pepper spray in Headwaters and the nunchaku pain compliance upheld in Forrester?
options: The nunchaku pressure was gradual and could be released the moment the subject complied, while pepper spray caused immediate searing pain that officers could not stop once the protesters agreed to release
There was no distinction; the court overruled Forrester
quiz.teach: The court stressed the officers' control over the force in Forrester and the uncontrollable nature of pepper spray, which could be relieved only by thorough flushing with water that officers delayed or conditioned on release.

quiz.q: What did the panel hold on remand from the Supreme Court in 2002?
options: That Lewis and Philp were entitled to qualified immunity because no prior case involved pepper spray on protesters
That the case must be dismissed

That viewing the facts for the protesters, the use of pepper spray on their eyes and faces was plainly in excess of the force necessary and no reasonable officer could have concluded otherwise, so Lewis and Philp were not entitled to qualified immunity
quiz.teach: Applying Saucier's two steps, the panel found a violation on the protesters' facts and held the unlawfulness clear, relying on the lack of any need for the spray, the available alternatives, LaLonde's rule on repeated use and refusal of relief, the manufacturer's distance warning, and statewide practice limiting pepper spray to hostile or violent subjects.
